title: Day 58 · Week 8, Day 2 — Physiology: her mouth — the bacterium that eats her hormones, the three trials that killed a seven-fold risk, and the bugs your child will catch from her at two
summary: The fifth Physiology episode. Your baby is at Carnegie stage 18 (13–17 mm; the NHS raspberry), the tibia's shaft turning to bone today behind the clavicle and femur, the elbow bending — and in a jaw the size of a rice grain, the dental lamina and the first twenty tooth buds forming (Hovorakova 2018), to mineralise from ~14 weeks (Lunt & Law 1974). Pregnancy gingivitis: 60–75% of pregnant women (CDC), peaking in the third trimester (ACOG CO 569), named by Löe & Silness 1963; inflammation rises through pregnancy without a rise in plaque (Figuero 2013, 33 studies). Why: leakier gum vessels, and Prevotella intermedia, which can substitute oestradiol or progesterone for vitamin K and grows on her hormones (Kornman & Loesche 1980, 1982; Jensen 1981). It is reversible and does not progress to periodontitis (Gürsoy 2008). Pregnancy epulis in ~5%; acid from vomiting is rinsed, not brushed, for an hour. Then the great story: a 7.5-fold odds ratio for preterm low birth weight (Offenbacher 1996, 124 women), 18 of 25 observational studies agreeing (Xiong 2006), 11.2% vs 28.6% preterm in OCAP (Offenbacher 2006, 1,020 women) — and three large randomised trials of deep cleaning in pregnancy that moved nothing: OPT (Michalowicz 2006, 823 women, 12.0% vs 12.8%), MOTOR (Offenbacher 2009, 1,806 women, 13.1% vs 11.5%), PIPS (Macones 2010, 757 women, RR 1.19), and the Cochrane review of 15 trials and 7,161 women (preterm RR 0.87, 0.70–1.10; no adverse effects). Why the dentist still matters: 40–50% of pregnant women have periodontal disease and 56% see no dentist; ACOG says X-rays with shielding and lidocaine are safe and treatment should not be delayed (Hagai 2015: 210 exposed pregnancies, anomalies 4.8% vs 3.3%, NS); free NHS dental care through a year after the due date. And the finding that outlasted the preterm hypothesis: decay is infectious, children acquire mutans streptococci in a window around 26 months (Caufield 1993), 71% from an identical maternal strain and never the father's (Li & Caufield 1995), children of mothers with untreated decay >3× more likely to have cavities (CDC) — and the Finnish xylitol trial (Söderling 2000; Isokangas 2000: colonisation 9.7% vs 28.6–48.5%, decay at five down ~70%). Plus the truth behind 'a tooth for every child' (Russell 2010: more untreated, not more total, decay).
action: Ten minutes tonight, two things. One: she books a dental check-up and cleaning for this trimester, says she's pregnant when booking, and asks for the usual X-rays with shielding; if the practice hesitates, the sentence is 'ACOG and the ADA say dental care in pregnancy is safe and should not be delayed.' In England, ask for the FW8 maternity exemption form at the booking appointment — the dentist is free through a year after the due date. Two: a box of baking soda and a cup go by the bathroom sink tonight, with the rule said once: after being sick, rinse, don't brush, for an hour. Optional: a packet of xylitol gum in the kitchen drawer for the habit the Finnish trial started after the birth.
